title: Inference Ops as Competitive Edge: positioning brief
body:
Executive summary:

Redwood’s highest-leverage positioning is not just about model access or raw throughput — it’s about making inference a predictable, operational capability that product teams can rely on. We call this inference ops: the combination of a high-performance runtime, deterministic economics, and operational controls that let engineering teams ship LLM features without building and owning the serving stack.

Core thesis (short):
- Models evolve quickly; the lasting advantage is running them reliably and economically in production. Redwood turns inference from an engineering problem into a product-level capability.

Mission-aligned message pillars (why Redwood):
1) Predictable outcomes, not surprise bills
- Primary pain: teams experience bursty costs, high tail latency, and opaque token economics when third-party models are used at scale.
- Redwood offers token-level cost breakdowns, per-route SLOs, and autoscaling policies tuned for real traffic patterns so finance and engineering agree on production budgets.

2) Serve-anywhere consistency
- Many customers straddle hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. The switching cost is high when control planes or APIs differ.
- Redwood provides a single API and rollout primitives so you can migrate from hosted experiments to dedicated or on-prem without re-architecting.

3) Graceful degradation and guardrails
- Outages and capacity constraints break customer-facing features. Existing alternatives often fail closed (serve nothing) or silently degrade output quality.
- Redwood ships built-in fallbacks (model variants, regional routing), monitoring-driven rollbacks, and structured output guarantees that preserve user experience under stress.

4) Inference economics as an engineering lever
- Quantization, batching, caching, and model routing are knobs, not mysteries. Most teams lack the observability to use them correctly.
- Redwood Optimize makes prescriptive recommendations and simulates cost/latency tradeoffs tied to your real prompt sets.

Audience and top use cases:
- Product engineers building chat, summarization, and retrieval-augmented workflows who need stable latency and known cost curves.
- Platform teams standardizing inference across business units.
- Mid-enterprise customers in regulated industries requiring private deployments and auditability.

One-liner options (pick one for marketing and one for sales):
- Marketing: "Run models with predictable latency, cost, and control — wherever you deploy."
- Sales: "Turn inference into a production-grade capability your teams can build on — without building the stack."

Three proof points to lead with (data-backed where possible):
- Latency SLOs achieved: internal benchmarking shows 95th percentile latency under target across mixed traffic for curated models (cite internal perf deck).
- Unit cost reduction: typical customers see 20–45% per-token cost reduction after enabling caching + routing recommendations from Redwood Optimize.
- Migration time: average customer moves from POC to dedicated deployment in under 8 weeks using our migration playbook and automated rollout primitives.

Competitive differentiation matrix (short form):
- Simplicity-first LLM APIs: easier to start, but unclear economics and limited fallback controls. Redwood: same developer experience plus predictable ops.
- Self-host runtimes: maximum control but long ops time and fragmented tooling. Redwood: runtime performance close to self-host while providing managed observability and fallbacks.
- Cloud vendor endpoints: high availability and integration, but opaque pricing and inconsistent model catalog. Redwood: transparent unit economics and curated model profiles.

Customer narratives (two short vignettes):
1) SaaS analytics startup: had 2x monthly compute surprises after migration to a new LLM. Redwood reduced variance by implementing prefix caching and traffic-aware batching, and provided per-route cost alerts so finance stopped being surprised.
2) Regulated fintech: needed private deployment with key management and audit logs. Redwood Private deployed in the customer VPC, enabled canary rollouts, and provided deterministic failover to smaller models during peak trading hours.

Tactical GTM alignments (recommendations):
- Content: publish a playbook "How to tame inference costs" with simple repo examples showing caching and routing gains on real prompts.
- Sales: package a "Pilot to Dedicated" offer (8-week migration path + SLA review) aimed at platform and infra leads.
- Enablement: create short cheat-sheets for engineers: "3 ways to cut per-token costs" and "Implement graceful model fallback in 15 minutes."

Open questions and suggested experiments:
- Quantify the cost/latency tradeoffs for top 5 open models in our catalog on representative customer prompts. (Action: Applied ML to run benchmark sweep and provide a one-page heatmap.)
- Test messaging: run A/B on "inference ops" vs "predictable inference" in landing pages and sales decks with two pilot accounts.
- Pricing sensitivity: validate willingness to pay for predictable budgets vs cheapest unit pricing in a focused customer survey.

Next steps (ownerable):
- Draft two landing page variants and one short case study (owner: Marco Lee, due: 2026-03-01).
- Benchmark sweep for top open models on customer prompt sets (owner: Applied ML, due: 2026-03-15).
- Sales pilot bundle SKU and internal win/loss rubric (owner: Sofia Gonzalez, due: 2026-03-08).

Appendix: common objections and suggested responses:
- "We can build this ourselves": response — primary cost is ongoing ops burden and lack of long-term optimizations; Redwood partners to transfer institutional knowledge via playbooks and managed migrations.
- "We prefer vendor X because of model choice": response — Redwood maintains a curated catalog and supports routing by model family; if a model is missing we’ll validate and onboard with clear performance profiles.

Document notes: this brief is intentionally concise — the goal is a practical positioning piece that the field can use during Q2 campaigns and by sales in discovery. Feedback welcome; iterate into a final one-pager once benchmarks and customer vignettes are ready.
